#9093. European Beauty Standards: Impact on Self-Image and Diversity

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins says about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of big butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal issues and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

Two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins says about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

“She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins says this concept can lend to beauty standards.

When it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins says you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in new people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

Coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins says change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins says, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.

6 standout designs that ruled the cinema screen this year.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I'm calling it. 2026 is the year of the movie title card. Also known as intertitles, these stylised film openers have existed since the silent movie era, showcasing a unique and iconic artistic legacy that rivals some of the best movie posters.

Title cards aren't just for aesthetics; they offer a narrative anchor, a beat to collect yourself before the action begins. But of course, it's. not empty imagery. The best movie title cards can be a storytelling device in themselves, and this year we've seen some stunning examples.

In contrast to the film's bold poster typography featuring sturdy sans serifs and clean composition, The Bone Temple's title card feels surprisingly organic. Created in a natural, hand-drawn scrawl, the imperfection of the lettering gives it an almost juvenile feel.

Appearing just after a particularly violent opening, the silent serenity of the title card scene regrounds the audience, offering a moment of respite from the chaos. But set against the temple of bones, there remains an eeriness to the blood-red hue of the title card typography,

A post shared by Warner Bros. Philippines (@warnerbrosph)

Championing hand-crafted design, Emerald Fennell's Wuthering Heights took a delightfully strange approach to title card creation. Made using hair (including some of the lead actors' real locks!), the stop-motion title card is equal parts whimsical and slightly disturbing, setting the tone for the madness that ensues.

"We wanted it to feel completely human", Fennell explains in a behind-the-scenes sneak peek. "It's really thrilling to show the hands that make something," she adds. Wonderfully tactile and hauntingly beautiful, the title card demonstrates how thoughtful design can effortlessly set the tone of a film.

A prime example of how simple title cards can create a sense of tension, The Drama's erratic opening plants a seed of anxiety amid the intimacy of the dance scene. Using a jumbled mix of script fonts, stately serifs and bold sans serifs, the chaotic nature of the title card signals a sense of chaos amid the calm.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Appearing only fleetingly, almost as if the screen is glitching, the random fonts create a sense of visual disharmony as they flash across the scene. Appearing in a conventional white colour scheme, the juxtaposition of order and disarray builds a perfect layer of discomfort.

Obsession demonstrates one of my favourite movie tropes – the integrated title card. After a particularly harrowing scene, protagonist Bear is seen weeping on his bed as a tense score begins to creep in. The camera pans down to reveal the Obsession title card woven into the duvet.

The simple visual effortlessly creates an eerie effect, as the viewer is thrown into the film's suffocatingly bleak universe. Purposefully domestic in nature, the tactile title card hints that the horror is not abstract or far away, but lingering under our noses.

Wildwood's beautiful title card was created by hand, using tactile design to breathe life into each letter form. With diverse natural wood textures, crawling ivy and powered pigment details, each human-made design has its own story woven between the branches.

With animation studio Laika heavily promoting its human-made artistry, it's no surprise this dedicated craft extends to its stunning title card. Demonstrating the beauty that comes from intricate, time-intensive work, Wildwood's title card shines as a rejection of the increasing quantity of AI slop taking over cinema.

Resident Evil title card. https://t.co/ZxxvIHJlthNovember 2, 2026

The Resident Evil title card is perhaps one of the most controversial on the list for an unexpected reason. With the franchise's origins stemming from the gaming world, many die-hard fans were anticipating the game's iconic title voice narration, something that director Zach Cregger opted against.

The tense, thumping score, paired with the rapid warping of the bold title card, creates an eerie effect that stands strong on its own (basically, doing away with the campiness of the game narrator was a good move). Grungy and terrifying, the title card perfectly encapsulates the film's decay into raw, unrelenting horror.

#9091. Andy Warhol’s ‘Camouflage’ Portraits Inspired Piaget’s New Limited-Edition Watch

Andy Warhol amassed quite the watch collection during his life—including a piece or two from Piaget (around seven, to be exact). And now, the maison has collaborated with the Andy Warhol Foundation for Visual Arts to bring an homage to the artist to your wrist.

Meet the Camouflage watch, a creation inspired by Warhol’s Camouflage self-portraits, which the artist crafted in 1986. As such, just 86 pieces of this iteration of the Andy Warhol watch will be made. Piaget takes the bold colors splashed across the American creative’s face in the series and plops them right on the dial. Here, sodalite and turquoise stones are the stars in waves of blue, paired alongside satin-finished gold and polished rose gold to add texture and dimension to that camouflage look. Piaget uses 27 pieces in all to make the dial, which it took over 100 hours of R&D and craftsmanship to come to life, into a blend of blue and warm hues. Related Articles Gagosian to Sell Works from Mr. Chow's Art Collection, Including Paintings by Warhol, Basquiat, Hockney, and More Miami Art Dealer Sentenced to Nearly Four Years in Prison for Selling Fake Warhols

Beating away inside the gadrooned white-gold case lies Piaget’s 501 P1 caliber, an automatic movement that powers those dauphine hands and offers up a 40-hour power reserve. Flip the watch over, and you’ll catch a glimpse of Warhol’s engraved signature, as well as the number of watches in the series.

“Our objective is to take inspiration from Andy Warhol’s creations without strictly reproducing each of his works on a dial,” Stéphanie Sivrière, artistic director of Piaget, said in a press statement. “The direct connection between Andy Warhol and Maison Piaget is color, particularly through the use of ornamental stones, which remains the common thread of this very distinctive timepiece.”

This isn’t the first time the duo has teamed up, either. In 2024, Piaget was given the go-ahead by the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts to rename its Black Tie watch (itself a reinvention of the iconic Ref. 15102, a 45 mm cushion-shaped timepiece Warhol owned) in Warhol’s honor. Under the new license, the maison was also able to craft one watch annually that pulled from the artist’s oeuvre. As a result, Piaget dropped the limited Collage timepiece back in 2025, home to blocks of pink opal, green chrysoprase, and yellow serpentine on the dial, now followed by the 2026 iteration (price available upon request). We’ll just have to wait and see what’s in the cards for 2027, then.

As part of Art Week NYC, a citywide gathering celebrating contemporary art, Jean-Bernard Forot, Piaget’s Head of Patrimony, is speaking with ARTnews senior editor Maximilíano Durón about Warhol’s love of timepieces and the watchmaker’s collaboration with the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts that grew out of it. The talk takes place at the PMC Studio on Saturday, November 14. RSVP here.

#9090. Scrapped marine rope recast as stools that rock like buoys

Rotterdam studio The New Raw has used discarded rope salvaged from the city’s harbour to create a series of 3D-printed public seating for its waterfront.

Called Buoy, the urban furniture project is shortlisted for a 2026 Dezeen Award in the sustainable design category.

To create the stools, The New Raw founder Foteini Setaki collected a series of plastic ropes from Rotterdam harbour, which were formerly used for managing boats and would’ve otherwise gone to waste.

The ropes were then transported to Maastricht, in the south of the Netherlands, where they were cleaned, shredded and mechanically recycled into pellets.

After returning to The New Raw’s Rotterdam studio, the recycled plastic pellets were melted and 3D-printed to create the stools, layer by layer.

“The material fuses as it is deposited, so no separate binder is needed,” Setaki told Dezeen.

Setaki explained that marine ropes are challenging to recycle because they contain a cocktail of materials that accumulate various residues over time.

Careful selection is essential to determine the ropes with the highest polypropylene content to be transformed into recycled plastic pellets, she explained.

While no virgin plastic is used in the creation of the stools, a small percentage of additives support the furniture’s long-term outdoor use, including UV protection.

“These additives are compatible with recycling the material again,” said Setaki.

Each seat features a subtly different hue, which is determined by the colour of the original rope rather than additional pigments or coatings.

The stools were also designed with spinning top-style pointed bases, so that they rock when the user sits down.

This gentle rocking motion was chosen to mimic real buoys bobbing along on the water.

“We wanted the seats to carry a recognisable link to their maritime origin, through both their shape and the slow movement of floating buoys,” explained Setaki.

“Borrowing that movement brings a playful quality to sitting, and the connection to the harbour becomes something you can feel.”

Each unique stool was engraved with its batch and production number, and then placed by Rotterdam harbour.

The project was created as an example of how designers can seek out local, surplus resources in an effort to contextualise their practice with the place that they work.

“Working with a local waste stream is a way of strengthening the relationship between the city and its harbour,” said Setaki.

“The material’s journey and the experience of sitting make that relationship tangible. This approach could also be adapted to other harbour cities, starting with their own discarded materials and local networks.”

Founded in 2016, The New Raw is run by Setaki and Panos Sakkas. The studio 3D prints locally sourced plastic waste to create furniture.

Buoy is nominated alongside a vibrant shortlist of sustainable design projects, including a cement-free architectural material made of waste date pits and lighting for an Australia bookshop made of its own faulty publications rejected due to printing errors.

Crafting a logo for a sports tournament is no easy job. It has to appeal to sports fans, who are notoriously conservative. It's going to have to work at tiny sizes, on a phone screen, and at massive sizes like a billboard or a stadium banner. The best sports logos manage all of the above.

It also has to make its point quickly and efficiently, because ordinary (non-designer) people are barely going to give it a second glance. So it usually pays to make the central visual idea blindingly obvious.

With this in mind, when I first saw the logo for the 2027 FIVB Men’s Volleyball World Cup, my reaction was: "Er… what that's supposed to be exactly?

Representing the tournament taking place in Poland next September, the logo emblem is a tall white shape with spikes at the top, a cluster of small squares in the middle and wavy stripes flaring out towards the base.

Perhaps I'm missing something, not being a volleyball fan myself. But to my eyes, it didn't look like... anything.

According to the press release, the inspiration was the World Cup trophy, whose “industrial form” has been distilled into a minimalist mark. And sure enough, when you look at the very distinctive trophy, it does look a lot like it. But it's not a pure representation, and that's deliberate.

Instead, four ideas are said to come together in the logo: the silhouette of the trophy, a circle representing the Earth, a sweeping curve representing the net, and reaching hands and a rising ball for the players. In the press release Maciej Bogusz, marketing director for the local organising committee, also added a fifth: the fans, represented by a wave rippling through the base.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Once you stare at the logo for a bit and pick out all these elements, yep, they're all present and correct. But that's kind of the problem: you have to stare to pick them out. All these concepts don't just magically mesh into one simple design; indeed, there are so many, that feels like it'd be close to impossible.

At the same time, it annoys the heck out of me when people judge a logo on first sight, because that's not how a logo should be judged. A logo is not primarily designed to be liked on first sight, it's designed to work over time.

The history of design is littered with logos that attracted a wave of negativity on first release, yet ended up being loved over time. And I don't want to make the same mistake here.

A post shared by Polska Siatkówka (@polskasiatkowka_official)

So here's something positive I can say: this doesn’t look like any other sports logo I can think of. There’s no generic shield, no generic ball with a swoosh, no cliches of any kind really.

Remember the London 2012 logo? It was widely ridiculed at first, but by the time the Olympic Games started, it had become a welcome part of the furniture.

This design now has plenty of time to do the same. Its first big outing is on 3 December, when the draw will take place 125m underground in the Wieliczka Salt Mine (because why not, eh?). And when the games start in Kraków, seven months later, the shape that looks so wrong to me may look, well, entirely right.

Honestly, I’m not convinced yet. But ask me again in September. My answer may be very different.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

#9087. President Trump Moves to Make Oval Office a Public Monument

President Donald Trump signed a proclamation Thursday seeking to designate the Oval Office and the adjacent Cabinet Room national monuments, saying that the new designation would prevent future administrations from making major modifications without Congressional approval. In his second term, Trump made it a priority to redecorate both, turning the previously restrained presidential working spaces into extravagantly gilded interiors in the style of Louis XIV.

In the immediate aftermath of this week’s midterm elections, in which his party suffered historic defeats, Trump appeared to be self-soothing by focusing on the many renovation projects he has initiated at the White House and across Washington, D.C. At the White House, in addition to his makeover of the Oval Office, these have included the construction of a granite helipad on the White House’s South Lawn and, most notoriously, the demolition of the building’s East Wing to make way for a 90,000-square-foot, $600 million ballroom. (On Wednesday, in his first public appearance after Tuesday’s Republican wipeout, Trump led a media tour of the ballroom construction site.) Related Articles After a Democratic Victory in Midterm Elections, Trump Focuses on Touting His Ballroom: 'This Is a Special Structure' In Fiery Court Filing, Democratic Lawmaker Says Kennedy Center's Closure Is Meant to Hide Its Failure Under Trump

Around the nation’s capital, Trump has embarked on a fraught, $14 million repair of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, begun the redevelopment of a popular public golf course by cutting down hundreds of trees, and proposed a 250-foot-high triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery. Apparently worried that incoming Democrats would block construction of the arch, Trump asked for hastened approval of the project, which was granted Wednesday by his hand-picked planning commission; that evening, Judge Tanya Chutkan stopped construction for fourteen days.

It is not clear how designating the Oval Office a national monument will prevent another president from simply revising, or ignoring, the designation—the White House itself is already designated a national historic landmark, which has not stopped Trump from building his ballroom. Nevertheless, speaking from the now gold-saturated Oval Office, Trump told reporters, “When completed, and when we get the documentation fully done, legally binding, it’ll make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space.”

#9086. Dezeen's favourite furniture and homeware from October

The first piece of furniture by architecture office Studio Hagen Hall and a pleated cabinet by Didi Ng Wing Yin feature in this roundup of design pieces spotted by Dezeen’s Jane Englefield over the last month.

Louis Hagen Hall of London-based Studio Hagen Hall has made his first foray into furniture with this sculptural coffee table, delivered as two legs and a weighty glass tabletop that require no mechanical fixings.

Hagen Hall originally designed the asymmetric piece for Pine Heath, a modernist Hampstead renovation with a corner sofa that required a bespoke coffee table to offset the negative space left by the seating.

Cherry veneer legs are paired with recyclable brown smoked glass to create the made-to-order piece, informed by the design philosophy of modernist American architect John Lautner.

Austrian, Netherlands-based designer Flora Lechner originally caught the attention of London’s Max Radford Gallery with her alternative aluminium chandeliers that look like ornate robots

Lechner has now translated her distinctive style into an unusual vase, composed of aluminium clips held together by stainless steel bolts. Stems can be slotted into the clips, which are supported by a base that can be filled with water.

“Exo 01 approaches the vase more as a support structure than as a container,” explained Lechner. “Inspired by braces used to hold and align parts of the body, the work applies this principle to flowers.”

Anne Holtrop is known for his rough-hewn furniture pieces, which conjure images of volcanic craters and mountainous landscapes.

For his inaugrual exhibition with Carpenter’s Workshop Gallery in London, the Dutch architect and designer is showing off his Low-relief collection of tables made from cast glass.

Their unrefined legs were informed by stone reliefs Holtrop visited in Aswan, Egypt.

Helsinki designer Didi Ng Wing Yin is known for his distinctively pleated wooden furniture, which he makes from locally sourced Finnish timber.

Last week, the designer debuted his first cabinet at Paris’s Spazio Nobile Gallery. Made from a mixture of fir and pine, finished with tung oil, the cabinet features a delicately pleated door made using Ng’s combined splitting, brushing and carving technique.

“I wanted to explore the dynamic contrast between form and texture,” Ng told Dezeen.

“The chunky pedestal base is built from straightforward architectural beams that retain their natural knots and raw characteristics, providing a heavy, structural anchor for the light, organic silhouette of the pleated cabinet door.”

One of many design events in October was PAD London, a collectible fair that takes place annually in Mayfair’s Berkley Square.

Among this year’s exhibitors was Mexico-based Manu Bañó, who showed a duo of striking patinated brass chairs formed from stacked, sculptural slabs of metal.

The chairs are a continuation of Bañó’s existing brass and stainless steel furniture, and were presented as part of the Objects with Narratives exhibition.

South Korean designer Seungjin Yang has been making playful furniture shaped like balloons for years, using colourful epoxy resin.

At PAD London, Yang showed his most recent balloon-like creations in the form of a sofa, two armchairs and two stools.

The designer coats real balloons in resin, painstakingly building their strength. Each piece is complete after around two weeks of delicate testing.

Don’t be misled by the intriguingly delicate appearance of Yang’s finished pieces, which are solid enough to be sat on.

#9085. Should I Exercise with a Phlegmy Cough? What You Need to Know

You’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Sleep is the best way to help your body recover quickly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Big disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

Stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

Light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing issues. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

Light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

Working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

An occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

Diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

The flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

Once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

They said they wouldn't do it. A touchscreen MacBook has been rumoured since the dawn of time (well, the noughties), but, in a quote that's been infinitely dredged up across the internet over the last couple of weeks, Steve Jobs himself decried the concept as "ergonomically terrible". But Jobs also famously asked, "Who wants a stylus?" And the answer among millions of Apple Pencil users seems to be a resounding, "Us!"

And after a few days with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, I'm happy to report that this is very much a device—perhaps even the ultimate device—for creatives. But rather than the ability to touch the screen, it's all about the quality of that 'PROLED' display itself. Turns out there's a reason Apple decided to lead with that, and not touch, in the name of the device.

Simply put, it's the best laptop screen I've ever seen. With up to 2000 nits of peak brightness, 10,000,000:1 contrast, and P3 + Adobe RGB colour, this is a best-in-class display that puts every other OLED laptop screen I've used to shame. It gives creatives a portable reference-quality display, which means it recreates video, colour and contrast as faithfully as possible. Once you've used the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, everything else looks washed-out in comparison, and for that reason alone it's impossible not to recommend for creatives – so long as the small matter of the $2,899 starting price isn't a barrier.

When it comes to touch, as I've written before, in my testing I've found it to be a nice-to-have rather than a need-to-have. Now that we're all touchscreen natives (which wasn't so much the case when Jobs made those comments in 2010), certain navigational actions just feel right, even on a laptop. Scrolling through windows, pinching to zoom in on a photo or map, scrubbing through the timeline in Final Cut Pro; there are plenty of times when touching the screen feels more intuitive than reaching for the trackpad. And Apple's subtle UI tweaks, such as having navigational icons expand when touched, make the whole thing feel more natural.

But equally, there were plenty of times when I preferred to use the trackpad – particularly when a certain level of accuracy was required. And despite Apple claiming to have produced a newly designed hinge with greater stability, it still wobbles. There's just no getting around the fact that a touchscreen on a vertical display is less ergonomic than it is on a flat one.

From a design perspective, the new MacBook Pro isn't a game-changer – unless you really missed the illuminating Apple logo (another noughties mainstay). There are improvements here and there; the Dynamic Island takes up less space than the notch, and slightly smaller bezels result in slightly larger viewing areas. But perhaps the most meaningful design change is the reduction in weight. That OLED panel has allowed for a 14% weight loss – making the 14-inch model, somewhat ironically, lighter than the 15-inch M5 MacBook Air.

But everything pales next to the screen. The PROLED XDR looks incredible. If you're looking for the most impressive visual fidelity available on a laptop, here it is. You can touch it if you like.

#9083. A New Hudson Valley Art Space Promises to Be As Accessible as It Is In Flux

Less than two blocks from the Katonah train station stands a nondescript, gray two-story building on one of the main drags of this Hudson Valley town. Emblazoned in a kerned-out serif font, its name, Branchline, belies what awaits inside: a public-facing exhibition space for the Gochman Family Collection (GFC).

Established just five years ago, the GFC has already become one of the world’s leading collections of contemporary Indigenous art, with more than 850 works. Until now, works from the GFC have primarily hung in the New York apartment of Becky Gochman, the collection’s founder and custodian, and her family, though some 200 works are typically on loan to institutions around the world at any given time. The GFC has generously opened the home to museum groups, schools, and artists for tours and events as a way to bring more attention to Native artists, but the organization’s ambition has always been to make its holdings as accessible as possible. Related Articles Leah Ke Yi Zheng Joins Antenna Space, Pérez Art Museum Miami to Honor Nicolas Berggruen, and More: Industry Moves for October 28, 2026 Elisa Nuyten's Vega Foundation Is Quietly Reshaping the World of Moving-Image Art

“It’s one thing to articulate a mission, but what matters to me,” GFC creative director and curator Rachel Martin (Tlingít) said Thursday during a press preview, “is if I’m putting that language out into the world [then] I’m making sure that our organization is following that with action.” She added that she sees Branchline as a place for “bringing community together, which means making the Native community feel like they are very much a part of what the decision-making parts of this are, and then also inviting the community of Katonah to come in and learn about new artists that they might not have heard of.”

Anticipating that many visitors will arrive via Metro-North, the GFC named the space after the rail term “branch line,” or the place “where paths diverge and new paths begin,” as GFC director Laura Phipps put it. “We were excited about all the sort of ideas that ‘branch line’ conjures—both thinking about the metaphor of the train and the metaphor of trees—and what we can do to experiment and grow in this space.”

Free to the public, Branchline is taking its time to grow into its new digs, which will eventually total 10,000 square feet across four buildings. Friday evening’s inauguration will show off the first completed space, as well as plans for expansion in the coming months across an L-shaped plot that runs from the main building’s entrance on the Parkway to Katonah Avenue. The building houses a three-room gallery on the ground floor, two bedrooms upstairs for invited artists to determine how they want to spend the time, and a nearly operational ceramics studio downstairs.

Architectural renderings on view Thursday afternoon show that the building’s back door will open onto a small sculpture deck leading to a yet-to-be-built barn, where large-scale works will go on view. (The original barn was in such bad shape that it had to be torn down to make way for an exhibition space.) The barn will in turn lead to the Annex, which will take a more experimental approach (more on that later). From there, visitors will turn left onto a patio and eventually reach the back entrance of Twig, a retail store and café.

For now, visitors will get a taste of Branchline’s ambitions through a more traditional offering. Inaugurating the modest, nearly 2,000-square-foot gallery is “Line Break,” curated by GFC assistant curator Moonoka Begay (Ndee + Diné) with collection associate Nicole van Brugge. “Lines are a core facet of all visual language,” the exhibition’s introductory wall text begins, but Begay and van Brugge look past the formal qualities that a line and its breaks contribute to a work. Instead, they treat the line as a metaphor for lineage and bloodlines, borders and cartographic marks, horizons and sound barriers.

A tight show of 28 works by 18 Indigenous artists, “Line Break” offers visually compelling juxtapositions of artists from different generations working in a range of mediums and styles. Jaune Quick-to-See Smith’s The Spaniard (1988), a semi-abstract aerial view of the Flathead Indian Reservation in Montana, hangs next to Sara Flores’s Untitled (Shao Pei Maya Kené), 2024, a painting rendered in the geometric abstract visual language of the Shipibo-Conibo people, whose designs, according to an exhibition brochure, “map the community’s local worldview, environmental understanding, and cosmology.” Farther along are Teresa Baker’s Echoes (2024) and George Morrison’s Night Shadows. Red Rock Variation: Lake Superior Landscape (1994). Both are brightly colored abstract meditations on landscape made in very different mediums: acrylic, yarn, willow, and artificial sinew on AstroTurf for Baker; acrylic on canvas on board for Morrison.

Even the most seemingly formal works reveal their secrets as you delve deeper into how these artists use lines to make meaning. Across from the Quick-to-See Smith and Flores works are two pieces from Nadia Myre’s “Code of Construction” series, in which the artist arranges strung ceramic cylinders into squares depicting the ground-to-air distress signals for “Require Map and Compass” and “Not Understood.” Myre’s choice of medium draws on the tradition of wampum belts, used by Indigenous communities of the Northeast Woodlands to communicate political relationships. Myre’s work finds an analog in Faye HeavyShield’s the red line II (2025), a strand of red beads that the artist strung by hand. Here it is displayed in a coil, though its configuration is flexible—perhaps a metaphor countering the seeming immutability of shape, form, and even time.

The exhibition reaches its crescendo at its center with Raven Chacon’s Storm Pattern (2021–24), a handwoven wool textile accompanied by a multichannel sound piece whose low hum visitors have been hearing since entering the gallery. In 2016, Chacon noticed the sounds made by drones flying over the Oceti Sakowin camp at Standing Rock, where protesters had gathered to oppose the Dakota Access Pipeline. Ranging from loud and piercing to soft and soothing, the sounds of police surveillance drones mingled and merged with those of the protesters’ countersurveillance drones. In that harmonious dissonance, Chacon saw a score, which he recorded and also translated into the woven textile, charting the drones’ erratic flight patterns in a traditional Diné weaving style and structure.

Rounding out “Line Break” are two elements that will likely look drastically different in a few months. The GFC commissioned Matthew Kirk to make a site-specific work for an exterior wall of the building along an alleyway. Across three plywood panels, Kirk has collaged painted tar paper in various abstract forms and shapes. The work was already showing its ephemeral quality on Thursday morning, the paper having warped in the light rain.

A few steps down the alleyway is the Annex, which is still under construction: the plywood is exposed, and power cords run to jerry-rigged lightbulbs that illuminate its two floors. Rather than hide this rawness, the GFC team has decided to embrace it. For now, the Annex is home to a small show of drawings by Shuvinai Ashoona, who maps imagined scenes—ones that could perhaps one day come true—onto the Arctic landscape where she lives in Nunavut, Canada. The team acknowledged that it hasn’t quite figured out how the space will look in the near term, even once the build-out is complete. That will depend on how artists interpret a prompt that gives them the autonomy to do what they want.

“What GFC is doing is not trying to become an institution,” Martin said. “It’s trying to just meet where things are needed, and a space is definitely needed for art that is outside of the white box that you’re used to seeing, so that’s what we’re offering.”

#9082. Tiered immigration hub by Aedas opens at Shenzhen-Hong Kong border

Photography courtesy of Aedas (unless stated otherwise)

Architecture studio Aedas has completed a tiered, round-edged building designed to accommodate an immigration hub between Hong Kong and Shenzhen, China.

Perched on the banks of the Shenzhen River, the New Huanggang Port Development opened earlier this month in replacement of the original Huanggang Port, which first opened between the two cities in 1989.

Conceived by Aedas as a “large-scale integrated hub”, the nine-storey facility combines border control and transport networks with 25,000 square metres of public space.

Its stacked volume is complete with a “flowing facade” formed of horizontal metal fins, while its rounded form was designed to evoke a pebble, in reference to its riverside location.

“The grounded, rounded form responds to the building’s large scale and waterfront setting, evoking a pebble resting on the banks of the Shenzhen River,” the studio told Dezeen.

“Flowing metal fins wrap the elevation like ribbons, reinforcing the building’s fluid appearance and symbolising the close connection between Shenzhen and Hong Kong.”

“[The building’s] integrated transport networks, flowing facade and welcoming civic spaces express the close relationship between the two cities while establishing a distinctive point of arrival,” the studio added.

A modular, prefabrication approach was employed to construct the building’s volume, which opens up at ground level via two sunken plazas and is topped with a solar panel-covered roof terrace.

Across its four elevations, its rhythmic horizontal fins have been lifted to form large glass curtain walls that draw daylight into the interior.

Inside, the hub’s transport, immigration and public programmes are stacked vertically and connected by a network of internal escalators.

To accommodate an expected average of 200,000 passengers per day, two of these floors have been dedicated to immigration halls complete with a “barrier-free” design.

Direct connections to transport networks are provided on the floors below, where the hub links to four of Shenzhen’s rail and metro lines to “support a seamless border-crossing journey”.

“Transport, immigration and public programmes are vertically organised under one roof,” the studio said.

“The nine-storey building uses vertical stacking to organise pedestrian crossing, vehicle crossing, public transport and civic amenities efficiently within a constrained site, separating passenger and vehicular flows while maintaining convenient connections between programmes,” it added.

A series of structural, arched columns informed by Shenzhen’s emblem flower – the Bougainvillea – divide the expansive interiors, which are illuminated by 73 roof skylights, facade openings and an integrated lighting system.

Nearby, RHSP has unveiled designs for a skyscraper with a “striking butterfly layout” and MAD has completed a series of boulder-like galleries across a green-roofed museum.

Photography courtesy of Aedas (unless stated otherwise)

#9081. Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

Ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

Now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a big-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

So, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s important to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

The same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

Some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

Beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

Thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

If you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health issues that go beyond your hairstyle.

Furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

Creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.

#9080. How Going Blind Made Doris Salcedo’s Art Bigger and Better

Doris Salcedo is best known for her moving “anti-monuments,” gigantic artworks—or sometimes negative spaces—that propose new ways to commemorate atrocities. Always, she focuses on the victims’ perspectives. Her best-known work, Shibboleth (2007), installed in Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall, comprised one giant, scar-like crack in the concrete, rerouting foot traffic in a manner that evoked the jarring disruption of borders more broadly.

The Colombian artist began working at such a monumental scale only after she began losing her central vision. At age 31, Salcedo was diagnosed with Stargardt disease, a rare genetic condition, and today she is legally blind, with only peripheral sight. Related Articles Sophie Calle, Doris Salcedo Among Winners of $105,000 Praemium Imperiale Award Doris Salcedo Deserves Better Than Her Current Fondation Beyeler Survey

In November, at White Cube Gallery in New York, Salcedo will premiere a sculpture that is the culmination of decades of this collaborative way of working—and huge in a way that could never be accomplished by one person. A full-sized house—at nearly 30 feet—has been woven entirely from human hair. When I visited, dozens of assistants were working across her three studios, tying knots in individual strands, a painstaking process. The resulting pattern resembles chicken wire or a chain-link fence.

Even working with such a big team, the process took three years. “To be thankful is not enough,” Salcedo said of the collective effort, adding that it could have easily taken 20 years to make on her own—and that she couldn’t spare that kind of time at her age.

As Salcedo led me through her studio—her own iconic salt-and-pepper curls rhyming with the looping locks lining the space—she told me that all of her workspaces were designed by the architect Carlos Granada. The two have been working together for 25 years. He is also the architect behind Fragmentos, Salcedo’s 2018 “anti-monument” commissioned by her national government to commemorate the 2016 Colombian peace agreement. Visiting the building in the heart of Bogotá, what at first looks like a typical modernist, single-floor gallery takes on new weight in the feel of its flooring: The textured tiling is made from firearms that once belonged to the Colombian guerrilla group FARC and were later melted down. Visitors walk right on top of these instruments of violence and fear, on tiles Salcedo made in close collaboration with 20 Colombian women who survived sexual violence during the conflict.

The work has an undeniably chilling effect. School groups flock to it regularly. Some critics, though, have found its message misleading, since several splinter factions are still active and thousands of fighters rejected that 2016 agreement. But for Salcedo, Fragmentos is not a static space: She regularly invites other artists whose work resonates to exhibit within its walls. When I visited, a crew was de-installing a sound installation by Hajrah Waheed that filled the space with movingly hummed songs of resistance. The work, titled Hum II (2023), is surprisingly affecting, unifying: You’re made to feel something of the song’s sentiments even if they’re in languages you don’t understand. Fittingly, the title means “we” in Urdu, Waheed’s mother tongue.

Like Fragmentos, Salcedo’s studios boast high ceilings. Her workspaces also feature glass brick walls and floating staircases: These are sparse spaces that enable her and her team to see what they are working on. As she walked me through, magnifying glass in hand, she pointed out that one of her studios is the same shape as the home she is building—a triangle atop a square, as if a kid drew a house. Eventually, we came upon the net-like hair arranged in sections like a gradient, growing darker and denser at the bottom. She let me touch it, and I was surprised to find it so sturdy and lightweight at the same time.

THE WORK-IN-PROGRESS MARRIED a complicated process to a simple shape. As we spoke, I found myself wondering about the latter—why a house? I found a hint in two books sitting on the surface of her desk, both of them scanned so she can see them on a screen in large print: Domicide: The Global Destruction of Home and Dreamhouse: Stories of Art and Shelter.

House is not her first work on the subject of the devastating effects of the global housing crisis. Uprooted (2020–22), her prize-winning work in the 15th Sharjah Biennial (where, as it happens, she met Waheed, a fellow prize winner), repurposed 804 dead trees into a mesmerizing, if uninhabitable, home. At almost 1,000 feet long, the work is meant to speak to the predicament of climate refugees. Her newer work, which takes the same shape, is about more deliberate displacement: specifically, “domicide,” which the authors of one of the books on her desk, J. Douglas Porteous and Sandra E. Smith, describe as the calculated destruction of homes. Explaining the impetus for her piece, Salcedo pointed to current conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza, Syria, and Sudan, where people are being violently displaced en masse.

With House, Salcedo wanted to show that, while the dispossessed are of course vulnerable, they are also resilient. Her meshy nets are fragile and flexible, yet they are also much stronger than they seem. Hair may be ephemeral, but she makes it structural and sturdy. It’s all inspired, she told me, by the ways that spiders make webs of silk, material they take from their own bodies. Pairing hair and home, she evokes the ways that bodies and buildings—like dignity and domesticity—are tightly bound.

SALCEDO LEARNED TO WORK WITH human hair from earlier pieces: “Unland” (1995–98) comprises tables severed and then rearranged such that they depend on dissimilar tables for structural support. As if personifying the balancing act, the artist intricately threaded the surfaces with hair, drilling tiny holes in the tables to insert locks she gathered from a local salon. But for House, given its magnitude, she decided to source hair online, learning to look carefully for certain certificates, as there is a lot of violent crime in the human hair trade.

Hair is not the only tricky material that will feature in her fall show. On an upper floor of one of her studios, more assistants were at work on objects of a smaller scale, all destined for display alongside House at White Cube. They were wearing jeweler’s glasses and using X-Acto knives to meticulously remove the starch from individual grains of rice. A team of architects and engineers looked on, huddled around a computer on a lofted level as they worked out the structure of the sculpture’s shape. “I’ve never had such a large team,” she explained as I took in the scene. At one point, she tried working with a renowned engineer who eventually stepped down, saying the idea was too complicated.

When an artist uses sculpture’s most stalwart materials like wood or bronze—as Salcedo has in the past—“the tools are already designed for you,” she said. House required more trial and error than she’s ever needed before—so it also required her biggest team yet. “I had to fabricate new tools and new ways of working,” she explained as we watched assistants drill minuscule holes in starchless rice grains before passing them along to the next station, where still other assistants would thread individual hairs through those tiny openings. They were assembling a kind of mesh, then forming it around damaged cooking supplies—bowls and pots and pans—to form Grains of Sorrow (2023–26), a reminder of what is lost to domicide besides simple structure.

If this sounds like an incredibly elaborate—and surprisingly elegant—way to speak to tragedy, for Salcedo, both beauty and labor are part of her point. She is cognizant of how her studio might provide jobs to those who need them, employing, for instance, 150 women from the Colombian countryside, where it is difficult for them to find work.

The decision to both scale-up and work elaborately is as conceptual as it is material: “My work has always been labor-intensive because in the Global South, labor is intensive,” she said. “It’s completely different from industrialized countries.” She meant this not only as a way to shine a light on contemporary conditions, but also as a retort to art-historical tropes: Modernity is too often narrated, she said, as if “no single person from the Global South participated. But we know all the labor and all the suffering created modernity.” She wants to combine the forms and traditions of European sculpture with painstaking labor to show the two were always intertwined.

I asked her about the role beauty plays for her; she replied that she’s received a lot of criticism on this matter. She maintained, however, that “in all the violence and terror I’ve been researching all my life, I think the abject part belongs to the perpetrator,” adding that “beauty has a lot to do with dignity”—something she wants to restore as she tells the stories of victims. Elegance is also a way to get people to really look: The stories she’s telling are almost always in the newspapers, but that doesn’t mean everyone stops to soak them in. Salcedo doesn’t want you to divert your eyes from the world’s horrors, so she goes to extreme lengths to make sure you can’t look away.

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

"Is Social Security taxable?" is one of the most common tax questions retirees ask — and the answer frustrates almost everyone: it depends. Depending on your total income, anywhere from 0% to 85% of your Social Security benefits can be subject to federal income tax. The tax was introduced in 1983, originally affecting about 10% of recipients. Today, because the income thresholds were never indexed for inflation, roughly 56% of Social Security recipients pay tax on their benefits.

The good news: even in the worst case, you'll never pay tax on 100% of your Social Security. The bad news: the formula for calculating the taxable amount is one of the most convoluted in the entire tax code. In this guide, we'll break it down into plain English, show you exactly how to calculate what you owe, and — most importantly — share strategies the FI community uses to reduce or eliminate the tax entirely.

The IRS uses a special formula called "combined income" (also called "provisional income") to determine how much of your Social Security benefits are taxable. Here's the formula:

Combined Income = Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) + Nontaxable Interest + Half of Social Security Benefits

The resulting number determines which taxation tier you fall into. Notice that the thresholds haven't changed since 1993 — they are not adjusted for inflation, which means more retirees cross into taxable territory every year.

Important: "Up to 85% taxed" does not mean you pay an 85% tax rate. It means 85% of your benefits are added to your taxable income and taxed at your ordinary income rate. If you're in the 22% bracket and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you'd owe 22% on $25,500 — roughly $5,610.

This is the most common Social Security tax confusion. When the IRS says "up to 85% of benefits are taxable," it means 85% of your benefit amount gets added to your taxable income and taxed at your regular rate. If your marginal rate is 22% and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you owe about $5,610 — not $25,500. The effective tax rate on your full benefit in this example is about 18.7%.

Let's walk through a real example. Meet Sarah: she's 67, single, retired, and receives $24,000 per year in Social Security benefits. She also has $18,000 in IRA withdrawals and $2,000 in municipal bond interest.

Step 2: Determine the Tier Sarah is single with combined income of $32,000, which falls between $25,000 and $34,000. She's in the 50% tier — up to 50% of her benefits may be taxable.

Step 3: Calculate the Taxable Amount The actual calculation involves comparing two formulas and taking the lesser amount. For the 50% tier:

Sarah adds $3,500 to her other taxable income. At a 12% marginal rate, that's roughly $420 in additional federal tax on her Social Security.

Beyond federal taxes, 13 states also tax Social Security benefits to some degree as of 2026. Each state has its own thresholds and exemption amounts:

The remaining 37 states and Washington, D.C. do not tax Social Security benefits at all. If you're planning where to retire, this is a meaningful factor — especially if you have substantial SS benefits combined with other retirement income.

The FI community has identified several strategies that can significantly reduce the tax bite on Social Security benefits. The key insight: since taxation is based on combined income, controlling your income in retirement is the lever.

This is the single most powerful strategy. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula. If you retire early (before Social Security age), you have a window of low-income years to convert Traditional IRA/401(k) money to Roth.

Example: Between ages 55 and 67, you convert $500,000 from your Traditional IRA to a Roth — paying tax at rates as low as 10-12%. When you claim Social Security at 67, your Roth withdrawals don't push you into a higher SS taxation tier. Instead of 85% of your benefits being taxable, you might pay tax on 0-50%.

The math is dramatic over a 25+ year retirement. Converting at 12% during early retirement to avoid 22%+ taxation on Social Security for decades produces enormous tax savings.

Every dollar of AGI pushes you toward the 50% or 85% taxation tiers. Strategic levers include:

Once you reach age 70.5, you can donate up to $105,000 per year directly from your IRA to a qualified charity. This satisfies your Required Minimum Distribution (RMD) without the distribution being included in your AGI. Lower AGI means lower combined income, which means less Social Security is taxable.

For charitably inclined retirees, QCDs are one of the most tax-efficient giving strategies available — they simultaneously reduce your income tax AND reduce the tax on your Social Security benefits.

Delaying Social Security from 62 to 70 increases your benefit by roughly 77%. But there's a secondary benefit: during the delay years, you have more room to do Roth conversions at low tax rates without Social Security benefits adding to your combined income. The combination of larger benefits and lower taxation on those benefits makes delay doubly powerful for tax optimization.

If you retire before claiming Social Security, you have a golden window for Roth conversions. With little or no earned income and no SS benefits, you can convert Traditional IRA money to Roth at the lowest tax brackets of your lifetime. Every dollar you convert is a dollar that will never increase the tax on your Social Security benefits. This window closes permanently once you start claiming.

A step-by-step walkthrough for estimating what you owe.

List your AGI from all sources: IRA/401(k) withdrawals, pension income, wages, dividends, capital gains, rental income. Get your total Social Security benefit from your SSA-1099 form.

Pro tip: Don't forget nontaxable municipal bond interest — it counts in the combined income formula even though it's not on your 1040.

Add your AGI + nontaxable interest + half of your Social Security benefits. This "combined income" number determines your taxation tier.

Compare your combined income to the thresholds: Single — $25K (50% tier), $34K (85% tier). Married filing jointly — $32K (50% tier), $44K (85% tier).

For the 50% tier: take 50% of combined income above the lower threshold (capped at 50% of benefits). For the 85% tier: the calculation is more complex — use IRS Publication 915 worksheet or tax software.

Pro tip: Tax software handles this automatically. If doing it by hand, IRS Publication 915 has the complete worksheet.

The taxable portion of your Social Security gets added to your other taxable income and taxed at your marginal rate. Check if your state also taxes Social Security.

For single filers, Social Security becomes partially taxable when combined income exceeds $25,000 (50% tier) and up to 85% taxable above $34,000. For married filing jointly, the thresholds are $32,000 (50% tier) and $44,000 (85% tier). These thresholds have not changed since 1993 and are not indexed for inflation.

No. Social Security benefits are not earned income. They are classified as unearned income for tax purposes. This distinction matters for things like the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), IRA contribution eligibility, and the Social Security earnings test (which only applies to earned income like wages and self-employment).

No — and this is why Roth accounts are so powerful in retirement. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula used to determine Social Security taxation. Converting Traditional IRA money to Roth before claiming Social Security can dramatically reduce the tax on your benefits for life.

Yes. File Form W-4V with the Social Security Administration to have federal income tax withheld from your benefits. You can choose 7%, 10%, 12%, or 22% withholding. This avoids the surprise of a large tax bill at filing time. State tax withholding varies by state.

Social Security benefits are included in the Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) calculation that determines Medicare Part B and Part D premium surcharges (IRMAA). High-income retirees can pay significantly more for Medicare — up to 3.4 times the standard premium. Managing MAGI in retirement affects both Social Security taxation and Medicare costs.

There have been numerous proposals to reform Social Security taxation, including indexing the thresholds for inflation, raising the taxable percentage above 85%, or eliminating the tax entirely. As of 2026, no changes have been enacted. The thresholds have remained unchanged since 1993, meaning inflation automatically pushes more retirees into taxable territory each year.

Yes, Social Security benefits can be taxable — up to 85% of your benefits may be added to your taxable income depending on your combined income. The thresholds are low ($25,000 single, $32,000 married) and haven't been adjusted for inflation since 1993, catching more retirees every year. The single most powerful strategy is Roth conversions during early retirement years before claiming Social Security. Every dollar in a Roth account is a dollar that won't push your Social Security into the taxable zone. Plan your retirement income sources deliberately, and you can reduce or eliminate this tax entirely.

#9078. Lacaton & Vassal wins Le Prix Charlotte Perriand 2027

The Créateurs Design Association & Awards has named Pritzker Prize-winning French studio Lacaton & Vassal Architectes the recipient of the Le Prix Charlotte Perriand 2027.

Lacaton & Vassal Architectes, which is led by architects Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal and known for its social housing designs, was recognised for contributing to contemporary architecture by transforming and improving existing buildings.

The Créateurs Design Associates (CDA) said the studio’s work improves “living conditions while preserving resources and architectural heritage”.

The duo said it was “very happy” to receive the award.

“Charlotte Perriand’s tireless pursuit of comfort, well-being, and the pleasure of the inhabitant and of everyday life, her modernity, and her political commitment to exposing poor housing conditions and to transmission and education remain profoundly relevant today and are a source of inspiration,” Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal said.

“Her manifest spirit of openness and freedom touches us deeply. We are very happy to receive this distinction.”

The architects founded their studio in 1989 and have since worked on high-profile projects such as the transformation of the Palais de Tokyo in Paris, the Nantes School of Architecture and the Cité du Grand Parc housing transformation in Bordeaux.

The latter, which was completed with Frédéric Druot and Christophe Hutin, won the European Union’s Mies van der Rohe Award in 2019.

Lacaton & Vassal Architectes’ other social housing projects include the renovation of the 1960s Tour Bois-le-Prêtre tower block in Paris, also in collaboration with Frédéric Druot, which was completed in 2011.

It also converted and extended a former shipbuilding workshop to create the FRAC Nord-Pas de Calais contemporary art gallery in Dunkirk.

The Le Prix Charlotte Perriand was established in collaboration with the family of the late architect and recognises practitioners whose contributions have advanced architecture and design.

“In awarding Le Prix Charlotte Perriand to Lacaton & Vassal, the CDA members recognise the care and imagination with which they approach the places people call home. Their work shows how much can be gained by understanding what is already there,” Créateurs Design Association co-founder Meredith Xavier said.

The award will be given to Lacaton & Vassal Architectes in a ceremony on 16 January 2027, at the Shangri-La Paris. Architect Kengo Kuma will also be honoured at the event as the winner of the Andrée Putman Lifetime Achievement Award 2027.

Lacaton & Vassal Architectes has previously won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2021, as well as the 2023 Soane Medal for architecture.

Last year, Lacaton won the 2025 Jane Drew Prize for women in architecture.

#9077. 10 Signs You Might Not Really Be in Love: How to Tell the Difference

Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing. Are you truly in love or just caught in a wave of infatuation? Sometimes, what seems like a heart-thumping romance may be a fleeting crush.

Wondering how to tell the difference? We’ve got you! Here’s a rundown of the 10 signs you’re not really in love.

Feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo? That’s pretty normal. But before you start planning your future or picking out matching Halloween costumes, you may wanna make sure it’s real love and not a case of a serious crush.

Here are some signs that you may not really be in love:

Caught up in the romance novel vibe? If you’re all about the feelings of being in love rather than who’s sharing your popcorn, it might just be that you’re smitten with the idea of love itself.

Time to check if your relationship is more about the fairy tale than the real person.

Chatting with your partner shouldn’t feel as shallow as a kiddie pool. If deep talks are tougher than pulling teeth and rarer than a unicorn, it’s a red flag.

Sticking to small talk about the weather and dinner plans suggests the emotional depth for a lasting bond might be missing.

When discussions about future plans feel as far-fetched as sci-fi adventures, they may reveal underlying doubts about the relationship’s viability.

If imagining a future together feels unrealistic or undesirable, it’s time to ask yourself why. Real love plans a future; infatuation lives for the weekend.

Remember when their sock on the floor was cute? If little quirks now make you more cranky than charmed, it might mean the love goggles are off, your feelings have shifted from affection to annoyance, and the reality check has bounced.

Love is seeing imperfections and adoring them anyway.

Feeling more at ease or more ‘yourself’ when your partner isn’t around is a telling sign. If you’re secretly throwing mini-parties when they leave the room, you need to stop and think. Real-deal love means missing their chaos when they’re gone, not celebrating the silence.

Shared values are the anchor of deep, lasting relationships. If your core values clash more than a polka dot and stripes ensemble, you’re in for a rough ride, as finding common ground could be challenging!

Lasting love grows from shared beliefs and mutual respect, not from opposing battle lines.

No respect? No future. Respect is as critical to love as air is to breathing. Without mutual respect, you might just be coexisting rather than genuinely connecting.

If you no longer admire or respect each other’s opinions and choices, sustaining a healthy relationship will be difficult.

If they’re out of sight and totally out of mind, that’s not just independence — it might be indifference. When love is real, you should long for their laugh or lame jokes when they’re away. Could it be that your emotional attachment isn’t as strong as it should be for a lasting relationship?

If your best moments are consistently away from your partner, your heart might not be in it to win it. Perhaps your relationship isn’t providing enough support or happiness.

True love enriches your life and doesn’t play second fiddle to your social circle. It’s time to evaluate where your emotional energy is invested.

Still window shopping while you’re supposedly locked down? It’s a sign you might not be all in. A love that lasts doesn’t keep a backup catalog — it’s too busy loving what it already has.

Knowing why you’re still scanning for alternatives can help you address what might be missing or unfulfilled in your relationship.

Are you genuinely in love or just in love with being in love? If you’re secretly thrilled when they’re not around, stuck in surface-level chit-chat, or dreading deep-future talks, these are cosmic signs that it’s rethink o’clock.

Don’t ignore the signals — tuning in now can save you heartache later and lead you toward a love that genuinely fulfills you.

Last medically reviewed on June 26, 2024

The MovinkPad 11 comes with the Pro Pen 3, a paper-like screen, and a protective case, and the bundle now costs less than the tablet alone.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I’ve tested a fair few drawing tablets over the years, and while the iPad is still the default for many digital artists, Wacom is clearly keen to lure creatives away. The MovinkPad 11 is one of its more interesting attempts, and this deal is a good excuse to take a look.

Wacom is selling the MovinkPad 11 with a case for £402.70 with the code CASE20 at checkout. That’s down from £469.96, a saving of £67.26 (around 14%). The tablet alone is listed at a discounted £429.98, so you’re paying less for the tablet and case together than for the tablet by itself. It’s a handy extra, too, on a tablet that’s made to be tossed in a bag and used anywhere.

The MovinkPad 11 is built around the Pro Pen 3, not a generic Android slate with stylus support bolted on. The 11.45-inch display has a 2200 x 1440 resolution and a 90Hz refresh rate, and the screen is etched glass. If you’ve ever drawn on the slick glass of a regular tablet, you’ll know it can feel like sketching on a bathroom mirror. The textured surface adds a little grip and feels much closer to paper.

The Pro Pen 3 offers 8,192 levels of pressure sensitivity and 60-degree tilt recognition, and it needs no battery or charging. Those numbers look good on a spec sheet, but what I notice more is how naturally it responds to light pressure and follows your strokes.

It runs Android 14 with 8GB RAM and 128GB storage, so you don’t need a computer. You can download drawing apps such as Clip Studio Paint, and Wacom includes a two-year Clip Studio Paint DEBUT licence.

It isn’t the most powerful Android tablet around, and the screen suits sketching and illustration better than big professional workflows, but for that exact art need, it's a better choice than an iPad Air. It’s a portable digital sketchbook, and at £402.70 with the case, it’s easy to recommend.

Wacom’s premium MovinkPad Pro 14 is now 14% off too, and with its protective cover, it's a similar deal, saving £140.05. As my MovinkPad Pro 14 review found, its gorgeous OLED screen and Pro Pen 3 make it a serious iPad alternative.
